rows.question: How long will you pay for a hotel if my house is unlivable after a fire?
rows.answer:
**Your policy pays extra living costs, such as a hotel, for the shortest time needed to repair or rebuild your home, up to a maximum of 12 months, as long as the fire is a covered loss.**

**What's covered:** If a loss covered under this Section makes the residence premises not fit to live in, we cover Additional Living Expense: any necessary increase in living expenses incurred by you so that your household can maintain its normal standard of living. A hotel stay would fall under this coverage. The policy pays only the *increase* in your costs over what you normally spend, not your whole living budget.

**How long it lasts:**
- Payment will be for the shortest time required to repair or replace the damage or, if you permanently relocate, the shortest time for your household to settle elsewhere, but not to exceed 12 months.

**How much is available:**
- The limit for Coverage D is 30% of the Coverage A limit. Coverage A is your dwelling coverage, so your exact dollar limit depends on the Coverage A amount shown on your Declarations page.

**If the fire was at a neighbor's home instead:** If a civil authority prohibits you from using the residence premises because of direct damage to neighboring premises by a covered peril, we cover Additional Living Expense for no more than two weeks.

**Things that could affect your claim:**
- **Intentional fires:** The policy excludes any loss arising out of any act an insured commits with the intent to cause a loss.
- **Protecting your property afterward:** The policy also does not cover loss caused by neglect, meaning failure of an insured to use all reasonable means to save and preserve property at and after the time of a loss.

The final amount and length of payment will depend on the facts of your claim, so keep your hotel receipts and talk with your adjuster.

rows.question: How long will you pay for a hotel if a wildfire destroys my house?
rows.answer:
**If the wildfire is part of a state of emergency declared by the Governor, Additional Living Expense (which covers costs like a hotel) can be paid for up to 24 months, with a possible extension to 36 months. If no emergency was declared, the standard limit of 12 months applies.** In both cases, the fire must be a covered loss under your policy.

**The standard policy (12 months)**
If a covered loss makes your home unlivable, we cover Additional Living Expense: any necessary increase in living expenses incurred by you so that your household can maintain its normal standard of living. Payment will be for the shortest time required to repair or replace the damage or, if you permanently relocate, the shortest time for your household to settle elsewhere, but not to exceed 12 months.

**California changes for declared emergencies (24 to 36 months)**
Your California endorsement replaces the 12-month limit when the emergency condition is met:
- If a covered loss relates to a state of emergency declared by the Governor, Additional Living Expense is payable for a period of up to 24 months instead of 12 months.
- For a loss tied to a Governor-declared state of emergency, we will grant an extension of up to 12 additional months, for a total of 36 months, if you act in good faith and with reasonable diligence and encounter delays in reconstruction beyond your control.

**Advance payment for declared emergencies**
If a covered loss relating to a declared state of emergency makes the residence premises uninhabitable, we will provide an advance payment of no less than four months of Additional Living Expense upon request.

**Dollar limit**
There is also a cap on the total amount, in addition to the time limits. The limit for Coverage D is 30% of the Coverage A limit. Your Coverage A (dwelling) limit is shown on your Declarations page. Your living-expense payments end when either the time limit or this dollar limit is reached.

**If your house isn't damaged but you're ordered out**
If authorities bar you from your home because of fire damage to nearby properties, a different rule applies. The base policy covers this for two weeks if the nearby damage was caused by a covered peril. In California, the two-week civil authority limit in HO-3 Section 2.5 is replaced with a limit of four weeks for California residence premises.

**What your time limit depends on**
- Whether the Governor declared a state of emergency for this fire. This decides whether you have 12 months or 24 to 36 months.
- Your Coverage A limit, which sets your total dollar cap.
- How long rebuilding or relocating actually takes. Payments run for the shortest reasonable time, up to the applicable maximum.

This explains what the policy language says. It is not a final coverage decision. Your adjuster will confirm how it applies to your claim.

rows.question: Can I get an advance on living expenses after a wildfire?
rows.answer:
**Yes, in California you can request an advance on living expenses after a wildfire, but only if the fire is a covered loss tied to a declared state of emergency and it makes your home unlivable.** In that case, if a covered loss relating to a declared state of emergency makes the residence premises uninhabitable, we will provide an advance payment of no less than four months of Additional Living Expense upon request.

**What this depends on**
- **Whether a state of emergency was declared** for the wildfire. Without one, the California advance payment rule doesn't apply.
- **Whether the fire damage is a covered loss** under your policy.
- **Whether your home is uninhabitable.** The advance applies only if you can't live there.
- **You have to ask.** The advance is provided "upon request," so contact us to request it.

**Related protections in California (each has its own conditions)**
- **How long living expenses are paid:** Normally, Additional Living Expense is paid for the shortest time required to repair or replace the damage or, if you permanently relocate, the shortest time for your household to settle elsewhere, but not to exceed 12 months. In California, the endorsement changes this. If a covered loss relates to a state of emergency declared by the Governor, Additional Living Expense is payable for a period of up to 24 months instead of 12 months.
- **Further extension:** For a covered loss relating to a Governor-declared state of emergency, we will grant an extension of up to 12 additional months, for a total of 36 months, if you act in good faith and with reasonable diligence and encounter delays in reconstruction beyond your control.
- **Overall dollar limit:** The limit for Coverage D is 30% of the Coverage A limit. Your actual amount depends on the Coverage A limit shown on your Declarations page.
- **Evacuation orders:** If you're kept out of your home by authorities because of fire damage to neighboring properties, the base policy covers living expenses when a civil authority prohibits you from using the residence premises because of direct damage to neighboring premises by a covered peril. In California, the two-week civil authority limit in HO-3 Section 2.5 is replaced with a limit of four weeks for California residence premises.
- **Belongings advance:** If your home is destroyed, in the event of a covered total loss of the dwelling relating to a declared state of emergency, we will offer a payment under Coverage C of no less than 30% of the Coverage C limit, up to $250,000, without requiring an itemized inventory.

This explains what the policy language says. Whether your claim qualifies will be decided when it is reviewed, so please contact your adjuster to request the advance and confirm how these provisions apply to your situation.

rows.question: What's my deductible for hail damage?
rows.answer:
**Your hail deductible is a percentage of your Coverage A (dwelling) limit, not a flat dollar amount.** The exact figure depends on which percentage is shown on your Declarations page, so check there to see which one applies to you.

**How it works in Texas**
- For loss caused by windstorm or hail, the deductible in HO-3 Section 6.1 is replaced by a deductible equal to the percentage of the Coverage A limit shown in the Declarations for this endorsement. In Texas, this endorsement replaces your policy's standard deductible for hail losses.
- The available percentages are 1%, 2%, and 5%.
- The windstorm or hail deductible will not be less than $1,000.

**Example:** If the Coverage A limit is $300,000 and the Declarations show a 2% windstorm or hail deductible, the deductible for a hail loss is $6,000. We will pay only that part of the loss that exceeds $6,000.

**You pay one deductible per storm, not one per item damaged.** The windstorm or hail deductible applies to the total of all loss payable under Coverages A, B and C combined that results from a single windstorm or hail event. All windstorm or hail damage occurring within any 72-hour period is considered a single event. That means damage to your home, other structures such as a detached garage or fence, and your belongings from the same storm is added together, and the deductible is subtracted once.

**Other things to know about hail claims**
- **Cosmetic roof damage is not covered.** Cosmetic damage means marring, pitting or denting that changes the appearance of the roof surface but does not prevent the roof from continuing to function as a barrier to water entering the dwelling, and does not shorten the expected life of the roof.
- **Report the damage within one year.** A claim for windstorm or hail damage must be reported to us within one year after the date of the windstorm or hail event, unless good cause exists for later reporting.

To find your deductible in dollars, multiply your Coverage A limit by the percentage on your Declarations page. If the result is under $1,000, your deductible is $1,000. Whether a particular loss is covered will be decided when your claim is reviewed.

rows.question: Hail dented my roof but it doesn't leak. Is that covered?
rows.answer:
**If the dents only affect how your roof looks, they're likely not covered.** Your Texas Windstorm and Hail Deductible Endorsement excludes "cosmetic" hail damage to roof surfacing. But "it doesn't leak" isn't the whole test. Whether the dents shortened your roof's expected life also matters.

**What counts as cosmetic damage**

The endorsement says we do not cover cosmetic damage to roof surfacing caused by hail. Cosmetic damage means marring, pitting or denting that changes the appearance of the roof surface but does not prevent the roof from continuing to function as a barrier to water entering the dwelling, and does not shorten the expected life of the roof.

The damage is cosmetic, and excluded, only if **both** of these are true:
- The roof still keeps water out (no leaks), **and**
- The dents don't shorten how long the roof is expected to last.

If an inspection finds the hail damage shortens your roof's lifespan, the cosmetic damage exclusion wouldn't apply, even with no leaks. An adjuster's inspection would decide this, and I can't make that call.

**If the damage turns out to be covered**

- **Roof age affects payment:** Loss to roof surfacing caused by windstorm or hail is settled at actual cash value, not replacement cost, if the roof surfacing is more than 15 years old at the time of loss. Roof surfacing 15 years old or less is settled under HO-3 Section 6.3. Actual cash value generally accounts for the roof's age and wear, so it typically pays less than replacement cost.
- **A separate hail deductible applies:** It's a percentage shown on your Declarations page. For example, if the Coverage A limit is $300,000 and the Declarations show a 2% windstorm or hail deductible, the deductible for a hail loss is $6,000. We will pay only that part of the loss that exceeds $6,000. Your amount depends on your own Declarations.
- **One storm, one deductible:** All windstorm or hail damage occurring within any 72-hour period is considered a single event. The deductible applies to the combined dwelling, other structures, and personal property loss from that event.

**Next step:** If you think the hail may have done more than change the roof's appearance, consider reporting the damage so it can be inspected.

rows.question: Is flood damage covered by my homeowners policy?
rows.answer:
**No, your homeowners policy does not cover flood damage.** The HO-3 form excludes flooding and certain related types of water damage, and flood coverage is available only through a separate flood policy.

**What's excluded**

The policy says we do not cover loss caused by: flood, surface water, waves, tidal water, or overflow of a body of water, whether or not driven by wind; water or water-borne material that backs up through sewers or drains or overflows from a sump pump; or water below the surface of the ground that seeps through a foundation, basement floor or wall.

**Options for this kind of water damage**

- **Flood:** You would need a separate flood insurance policy.
- **Sewer or drain backup and sump pump overflow:** Your homeowners policy doesn't cover this on its own, but water backup coverage is available by endorsement with a sublimit. A sublimit means a smaller dollar cap applies to this coverage. Whether you have this endorsement, and its limit, would be shown on your policy's Declarations page.

**Related benefits also don't apply to flood**

Some extra benefits in your policy apply only when the damage comes from a covered peril, meaning a cause of loss the policy covers. Flood is excluded, so these generally wouldn't apply to flood damage:

- **Additional living expenses:** These are covered if a loss covered under this Section makes the residence premises not fit to live in.
- **Emergency repairs:** The policy pays for measures like tarping only to protect covered property that is damaged by a covered peril from further damage.
- **Debris removal:** This is paid if a covered peril causes the loss.

This is an explanation of the policy wording, not a final decision on any particular claim. If you're unsure whether your damage counts as "flood" or another type of water damage, contact your agent or claims representative.

rows.question: Does my homeowners policy cover earthquakes?
rows.answer:
**Generally, no. Your standard homeowners policy does not cover earthquake damage unless you bought separate earthquake coverage.** The policy says we do not cover loss caused by earth movement, including earthquake, landslide, mudflow, sinkhole, or subsidence, regardless of any other cause contributing to the loss.

**Exception for fire or explosion:** We do cover direct loss by fire or explosion that results from earth movement. For example, if an earthquake causes a fire that damages your home, the fire damage may be covered. The shaking damage itself is not.

**Adding earthquake coverage:** Earthquake coverage may be purchased separately by endorsement. Whether you're covered depends on whether you bought that endorsement. To find out, check your Declarations page or ask your agent. The documents I have don't include the terms of an earthquake endorsement, so I can't tell you what it would cover or what its limits or deductible would be.

This explains what the policy language says. It isn't a coverage decision on a specific claim.

rows.question: Is mold covered?
rows.answer:
**Mold is covered only in limited cases.** It must result from a covered peril, like a sudden pipe burst, and there is a $10,000 total cap.

**What the policy says**

Your homeowners policy (HO-3, §3.4) states: We will pay up to $10,000 in total for direct physical loss caused by fungi, mold, wet or dry rot, or bacteria, including the cost to remove it and to tear out and replace covered property to gain access, but only when the fungi or rot results from a covered peril, such as a sudden pipe burst. This is the most we will pay regardless of the number of locations or claims during the policy period.

In practice:
- **What's included:** Removing the mold, plus tearing out and replacing covered parts of your home to reach it. This applies only when the mold comes from a covered peril, and only up to $10,000 total.
- **What decides coverage:** The cause of the mold. Mold from a covered event, such as a sudden pipe burst, may be covered. Mold that didn't come from a covered peril isn't covered under this section. I don't know what caused your mold, so I can't say which situation applies.
- **The cap:** The $10,000 is a total for the whole policy period. It is not per claim or per location.

**Helpful tip:** If the damage comes from a covered peril, the policy also will pay the reasonable cost incurred by you for necessary measures taken solely to protect covered property that is damaged by a covered peril from further damage. For example, you might dry out or seal off a leak to keep mold from spreading. Keep receipts for these expenses.

This is what the policy language says, not a final coverage decision. An adjuster would review the cause of the mold to determine whether a claim is covered.

rows.question: My jewelry was stolen. How much will you pay?
rows.answer:
Under the standard homeowners policy (HO-3), theft of jewelry is capped at a special limit of $1,500 per loss for all stolen jewelry combined, unless you added extra coverage for specific pieces. This is a summary of the policy language, not a final claim decision.

**The jewelry theft limit**
- Your personal property coverage (Coverage C) has special limits for certain categories. These limits apply to each loss for all property in each category.
- For jewelry, the limit is $1,500 for loss by theft of jewelry, watches, furs, and precious and semiprecious stones.
- So if several pieces were stolen in one theft, the $1,500 cap applies to all of them together, not to each piece.

**If you scheduled your jewelry**
- Higher limits for scheduled items are available by endorsement. If you bought that kind of endorsement for particular pieces, its limits may apply to those items instead of the $1,500 cap. Check your Declarations page or ask your agent whether you have one.

**What I can't tell you**
The documents I have don't show your deductible or how a stolen item's value is calculated. The amount you actually receive could therefore be less than $1,500, depending on those terms and on the claim review.

rows.question: How much cash is covered if it's destroyed in a fire?
rows.answer:
**The most the policy pays for cash is $200 per loss.** Your homeowners policy (Form HO-3) has a special limit: The following special limits apply to each loss for all property in each category: $200 on money, bank notes, gold other than goldware, and coins.

What this means for you:

- **It's a cap, not a guaranteed amount.** If $1,000 in cash burned, the policy would still pay no more than $200 for it. That limit covers all of your cash, bank notes, and coins together in a single loss, not $200 for each item.
- **It isn't specific to fire.** The limit applies to each loss, so the same $200 cap applies whatever the cause of loss.
- **It falls under your personal property coverage.** Cash counts as personal property under Coverage C. The limit for Coverage C is 50% of the Coverage A limit unless a different limit is shown in the Declarations. The $200 cap on cash applies within that overall limit.
- **Some cash may not be at your home.** If the cash was kept at another residence you own rather than your main home, a different limit applies. Personal property usually located at an insured's residence other than the residence premises is limited to 10% of the Coverage C limit or $1,000, whichever is greater. The $200 special limit on cash would still apply.

The documents I have don't list higher limits for cash specifically. They only say that higher limits for scheduled items are available by endorsement. For the final amount of any claim, including whether your deductible applies, check your Declarations page or speak with your agent or adjuster.

rows.question: A windstorm knocked a tree onto my house. Will you pay to remove it?
rows.answer:
**Your HO-3 policy language provides for tree removal in this situation, up to set limits.** It pays up to $1,000 in total for the removal of trees felled by windstorm, hail or weight of ice, snow or sleet, with no more than $500 for any one tree, if the tree damages a covered structure or blocks a driveway. A tree that fell on your house would generally fall under "damages a covered structure," but the claims review makes the final decision.

**Other points to know:**

- **Damage to your house and debris from it:** Repairs to your home are handled separately from the tree removal. The policy also covers cleanup of damaged parts of your home. We will pay your reasonable expense for the removal of debris of covered property if a covered peril causes the loss. This expense is included in the limit of liability that applies to the damaged property. If the amount to be paid for the actual damage plus debris removal exceeds the limit, an additional 5% of that limit is available for debris removal.
- **Replacing the tree itself:** The policy won't pay to replace the tree. We do not cover loss caused by windstorm to trees, shrubs or plants.
- **Deductible:** We will pay only that part of the total of all loss payable that exceeds the deductible amount shown in the Declarations. A separate windstorm or hail deductible may apply if shown by endorsement. Check your Declarations page to see which deductible applies to your windstorm claim.

This explains what the policy language says. It is not a final coverage decision. An adjuster will review the details of your claim.

rows.question: A pipe has been slowly leaking under my sink for a month. Am I covered?
rows.answer:
**Probably not for the leak itself, though some resulting water damage may still be covered.** Because your leak has gone on for about a month, it falls under a specific exclusion in your policy. A separate provision may cover some of the damage the water caused, and the final decision rests with the claim review.

**Why the leak itself likely isn't covered**
Your policy covers direct physical loss to your home and other structures, but lists exceptions. One is continuous or repeated seepage or leakage of water or steam over a period of 14 or more days from within a plumbing, heating or air conditioning system or household appliance. A month-long slow leak under a sink matches that description.

**What may still be covered**
The same section says if any of these cause water damage not otherwise excluded, we cover the resulting water damage, including the cost of tearing out and replacing part of the building to access the system, but not the system or appliance itself. So:
- The pipe itself would not be covered.
- Water damage to the cabinet, floor, or walls might be covered, but only if that damage isn't excluded somewhere else in the policy. Section 5 (Exclusions) isn't included in what I have, so I can't confirm this.

**Mold or rot**
If the leak caused mold or rot, the policy pays up to $10,000 in total, but only when the fungi or rot results from a covered peril, such as a sudden pipe burst. A slow leak lasting more than 14 days is listed as an exception, so mold from it may not qualify.

**Belongings stored under the sink**
Your personal property is covered only for specific listed causes, which include accidental discharge or overflow of water or steam. Whether a slow leak counts for your belongings would be decided when the claim is reviewed.

**Next steps**
- Report the leak promptly and stop it if you can.
- Take photos of the damage.
- An adjuster will review the facts, including how long the leak lasted and what was damaged.

This explains what your policy says. It isn't a coverage decision or a promise of payment.

rows.question: How long do I have to send a proof of loss?
rows.answer:
**Under the homeowners policy (HO-3), you have 60 days after we ask for it to send your proof of loss.** The clock starts when we request it, not on the date of the loss. The policy says you must send to us, within 60 days after our request, your signed, sworn proof of loss.

**What to keep in mind**
- The proof of loss must be **signed and sworn**.
- It's one of several things you need to do after a loss. You also need to give prompt notice to us or our agent and prepare an inventory of damaged personal property showing the quantity, description, actual cash value and amount of loss, with bills, receipts and related documents.
- Sending it starts the payment timeline. Loss will be payable 60 days after we receive your proof of loss and an agreement is reached, a final judgment is entered, or an appraisal award is filed with us.

**If this is an auto claim:** The Personal Auto Policy section I have doesn't set a proof-of-loss deadline. It does require that we must be notified promptly of how, when and where the accident or loss happened, and that you promptly send us copies of any notices or legal papers received in connection with the accident or loss.

Your state may have an endorsement that changes these timeframes. Since no state was specified, this answer reflects only the standard policy language.

rows.question: Will you pay replacement cost or actual cash value for my roof repair?
rows.answer:
**Generally replacement cost, but only if your dwelling is insured for at least 80% of its full replacement cost at the time of loss, and only after the repair is actually done.** Until then, you'd receive actual cash value. This assumes the roof damage is covered and that the roof is part of the insured building. The excerpts I have don't mention roofs by name, and I can't confirm the cause of loss is covered.

**How it works for buildings**

- **The basic rule:** Buildings under Coverage A or B are settled at replacement cost without deduction for depreciation, subject to the conditions below.
- **If you're insured for 80% or more of replacement cost:** if, at the time of loss, the amount of insurance on the damaged building is 80% or more of its full replacement cost, we will pay the cost to repair or replace, up to the limit of liability.
- **If you're insured for less than 80%:** we will pay the greater of the actual cash value of the damaged part or that proportion of the cost to repair or replace that the limit of insurance bears to 80% of the replacement cost.
- **Before repairs are finished:** We will pay no more than actual cash value until actual repair or replacement is complete.
- **Claiming in two steps:** You may make a claim on an actual cash value basis and then make a claim for any additional replacement cost within 180 days after the loss.

**What the terms mean**

- **Replacement cost** is the cost to repair or replace damaged property with material of like kind and quality, for the same use, without deduction for depreciation.
- **Actual cash value** is the cost to repair or replace damaged property with property of like kind and quality, less a deduction for depreciation, including physical deterioration and obsolescence. For an older roof, that deduction can be significant.

**What it depends on**

1. **Your coverage amount compared with your home's full replacement cost.** Check the dwelling limit on your Declarations page. If it's below 80% of what it would cost to rebuild your home, your payment may be reduced.
2. **Whether you complete the repair.** You'll get the full replacement cost only once the repair is done, and you must claim the additional amount within 180 days after the loss.
3. **Whether the damage itself is covered.** I don't have information about what caused the damage.

This explains what the policy language says. It is not a coverage decision. Your adjuster will determine coverage and payment based on the facts of your claim.

rows.question: I disagree with the adjuster's estimate. What can I do?
rows.answer:
**If this is a homeowners (HO-3) claim, you can demand an appraisal, a process where independent appraisers settle the dollar amount of the loss.** The policy says that if you and we fail to agree on the amount of loss, either may demand an appraisal of the loss.

**How appraisal works under the homeowners policy**
- **Choosing appraisers:** Each party will choose a competent and impartial appraiser within 20 days after receiving a written request from the other. Make your request in writing.
- **The umpire:** The two appraisers will choose an umpire.
- **The decision:** A decision agreed to by any two will set the amount of loss.
- **Costs:** Each party pays its own appraiser and shares equally the expense of the umpire.

Appraisal decides how much the loss is worth. The sources shown don't say it decides whether something is covered.

**Payment timing**
Loss will be payable 60 days after we receive your proof of loss and an agreement is reached, a final judgment is entered, or an appraisal award is filed with us. Keep up with your own duties after a loss too. For example, you must send to us, within 60 days after our request, your signed, sworn proof of loss. You should also have an inventory of damaged personal property showing the quantity, description, actual cash value and amount of loss, with bills, receipts and related documents.

**A possible reason the estimate is lower than you expected**
If the dispute involves your belongings, personal property, awnings, carpeting, household appliances and outdoor antennas are settled at actual cash value at the time of loss but not more than the amount required to repair or replace, unless a Personal Property Replacement Cost endorsement is shown in the Declarations. Check your Declarations page to see whether you have that endorsement.

Also, we will pay only that part of the total of all loss payable that exceeds the deductible amount shown in the Declarations. In addition, a separate windstorm or hail deductible may apply if shown by endorsement.

**If this is an auto claim**
The auto policy section available to me doesn't describe an appraisal process. It explains how the loss is valued: Our limit of liability for loss will be the lesser of the actual cash value of the stolen or damaged property, or the amount necessary to repair or replace the property with other property of like kind and quality. If your car is a total loss, an adjustment for depreciation and physical condition will be made in determining actual cash value. For options on an auto dispute, contact your agent or the claims department.

This explains what the policy language says. It isn't a decision on your claim or a promise of any payment amount.

rows.question: How long do I have to sue the insurance company?
rows.answer:
**Under the homeowners policy (HO-3), you must start a lawsuit within two years after the date of loss, and only if you have first fully complied with the policy's terms.** The policy says no action can be brought against us unless there has been full compliance with all of the terms under this Section and the action is started within two years after the date of loss.

In practice, this means:
- **The clock starts on the date of loss**, meaning the day the damage happened, not the day you filed your claim or got a decision.
- **You must have met your duties under the policy first.** The two-year window applies only if you have fully complied with the policy's conditions, such as the steps required after a loss.

**Related deadline:** If you're claiming damage to your home or other structures and you accept an actual cash value payment first, you may make a claim on an actual cash value basis and then make a claim for any additional replacement cost within 180 days after the loss. That deadline is separate from, and shorter than, the deadline for filing a lawsuit.

**If your question is about an auto policy:** The auto policy sections I have don't include a deadline for suing. They do say we have no duty to provide coverage under this policy unless there has been full compliance with the following duties, including prompt notice of the accident and cooperation with the investigation. For the auto lawsuit deadline, check your full auto policy or contact us.

Your state's law may also affect these deadlines. Since no state was specified, this answer reflects only the standard policy language. For advice about your specific situation, consider talking with an attorney.

rows.question: How long do I have to sue the insurance company?
rows.answer:
**In California, you generally have two years from the date of loss to file a lawsuit, but that clock is paused from when you report the claim until the company formally denies it in writing.**

**The basic rule (HO-3 policy):** No action can be brought against us unless there has been full compliance with all of the terms under this Section and the action is started within two years after the date of loss. This means you also need to have met the policy's requirements before you can sue.

**What changes in California:** Your California endorsement modifies this rule, and it controls for California policies. It says the two-year period to bring an action is tolled from the time you give notice of the claim until we formally deny the claim in writing. "Tolled" means the clock stops running.

**Example:**
1. A loss happens, and the two-year clock starts.
2. You report the claim, and the clock pauses.
3. The company formally denies the claim in writing, and the clock starts running again.

The time between your report and the written denial doesn't count toward the two years. Reporting your claim promptly therefore preserves more of your time.

This explains what the policy language says. It isn't legal advice or a decision on any particular claim. If you're thinking about suing, consider talking with an attorney about your specific deadline.

rows.question: A guest slipped on my stairs. Will you pay their medical bills?
rows.answer:
**Your homeowners policy includes coverage that can pay a guest's medical bills after an accident at your home, but it has conditions and a limit.** This is Coverage F – Medical Payments to Others. I can't confirm that a specific bill will be paid. Your claim will be reviewed.

**What the policy says**

- **Who and where:** The policy pays the necessary medical expenses that are incurred or medically ascertained within three years from the date of an accident causing bodily injury, to a person on the insured location with the permission of an insured. A guest you invited who slipped on your stairs fits this description.
- **Time limit:** The guest's medical expenses must be incurred or medically ascertained within three years from the date of the accident.
- **Who is not covered:** This coverage does not apply to you or regular residents of your household. If the "guest" actually lives with you, this coverage wouldn't apply.
- **How much:** The limit is shown in the Declarations and is typically $1,000 or $5,000 per person. Check your Declarations page for your actual limit.

**What it depends on**

- Whether the guest was on your property with your permission (or permission from someone else insured under the policy)
- Whether the guest is a regular resident of your household
- The Medical Payments limit on your Declarations page, which caps the payment per person

If you'd like to start a claim, contact us or your agent with the date of the accident and the guest's information.

rows.question: Am I covered if I crash while driving for Uber?
rows.answer:
**It depends on whether your policy includes a Ride-Share and Delivery endorsement.** Without it, your policy provides no coverage while you're logged on to the Uber app. This policy does not provide any coverage while your covered auto is being used to transport passengers or deliver goods for compensation through a transportation network company or delivery platform, from the time the driver logs on to the platform until the time the driver logs off, unless a Ride-Share and Delivery endorsement is shown in the Declarations.

**What this means for you:**
- **Check your Declarations page.** This is the summary page of your policy. If a Ride-Share and Delivery endorsement is listed there, the "no coverage" rule above doesn't apply in the same way. I don't have the endorsement's terms, so I can't tell you what it covers or what limits apply.
- **The time window matters.** The exclusion applies from the moment you log on to the app until you log off. It applies whether you're carrying a passenger, delivering, or waiting for a request.

**Other related exclusions in your policy:**
- **Damage to your car:** The policy won't pay for loss to your covered auto which occurs while it is being used as a public or livery conveyance.
- **Medical payments:** Medical Payments Coverage doesn't apply to bodily injury sustained while occupying your covered auto when it is being used as a public or livery conveyance.

I can't make a final coverage decision. That depends on your actual Declarations page and the facts of the accident. If you drive for Uber, contact your agent or Cobalt Harbor Mutual to confirm whether you have the Ride-Share and Delivery endorsement. If you don't, ask about adding it.

rows.question: My car was stolen. Will you pay for a rental car?
rows.answer:
**Your policy can help with temporary transportation costs, such as a rental, if your car was totally stolen. The standard benefit is up to $20 per day, with a $600 maximum, starting 48 hours after the theft.** A larger benefit may apply if you bought Rental Reimbursement coverage.

**What the policy says**

- **How much:** In addition to our limit of liability, we will pay, without application of a deductible, up to $20 per day, to a maximum of $600, for temporary transportation expenses incurred by you because of the total theft of your covered auto. No deductible applies to this benefit, but it applies only when the car itself was stolen.
- **When it starts and stops:** We will pay only expenses incurred during the period beginning 48 hours after the theft and ending when your covered auto is returned or we pay for its loss. Rental costs from the first two days after the theft wouldn't be covered under this benefit.
- **If you have Rental Reimbursement coverage:** If a Rental Reimbursement endorsement is shown in the Declarations, its daily and maximum limits apply instead. Check your Declarations page, the summary page of your policy, to see whether you have this coverage and what its limits are.

**Something you need to do**

If your car is stolen, the policy requires you to promptly notify the police if your covered auto or any non-owned auto is stolen. If you haven't filed a police report yet, do so as soon as possible.

**What it depends on**

Whether this applies to your claim depends on a few things:
- whether the car was totally stolen rather than just broken into
- whether it's listed as a covered auto on your policy
- whether your Declarations page shows a Rental Reimbursement endorsement

This explains what the policy language says. It isn't a final decision on your claim. Your adjuster will confirm what's covered.

rows.question: I hit a deer. Is that collision or comprehensive?
rows.answer:
**Hitting a deer counts as comprehensive, not collision.** Your policy lists contact with bird or animal as a loss that is considered other than collision (comprehensive).

**What this means for you:**

- **You need comprehensive coverage on your policy.** The policy will pay for damage to your car caused by other than collision, only if the Declarations indicate that Other Than Collision Coverage is provided. Check your Declarations page, the summary page that lists your coverages, to confirm you have it. If you carry only collision coverage, this type of loss would not fall under it.
- **A deductible will apply.** Covered damage is paid minus any applicable deductible shown in the Declarations. Your comprehensive deductible amount is listed on your Declarations page, and it may differ from your collision deductible.

This explains how the policy language classifies your loss. It is not a final coverage decision. Whether and how much is paid depends on your Declarations and the details of your claim.

rows.question: I just bought a second car. How long do I have to add it to my policy?
rows.answer:
**You have 14 days from the day you became the owner to ask us to add your second car.** If it is an additional vehicle, coverage begins on the date you become the owner, but you must ask us to insure it within 14 days after you become the owner.

**What this means for you:**
- **What counts as a "newly acquired" car:** A newly acquired auto is one you become the owner of during the policy period.
- **When the clock starts:** The 14 days count from the date you became the owner, not from when you picked up the car or registered it.
- **Coverage in the meantime:** For an additional car, coverage starts on the date you become the owner, but only if you contact us within that 14-day window.

**If the new car is replacing a car on your policy:** A different rule applies. If it replaces a vehicle shown in the Declarations, it has the same coverage as the vehicle it replaced, and you must ask us to insure it within 14 days only if you wish to add or continue Physical Damage coverage. Physical Damage coverage pays for damage to your own car.

Your exact coverage depends on your policy details, so contact us as soon as you can to add the car and confirm your coverage.

Your policy's Uninsured Motorist coverage can apply to hit-and-run accidents, but only when certain conditions are met. A hit-and-run vehicle counts as an "uninsured motor vehicle" only if it is one whose operator or owner cannot be identified and which hits you, a family member, or a vehicle you or a family member are occupying. The Uninsured Motorist insuring agreement covers injuries to people. rows.question: What's my reserve authority as an associate adjuster?
rows.answer:
As a Level 1 (Associate Adjuster), your standard reserve authority is **$25,000 per claim**. A temporary increase applies only during a declared catastrophe for windstorm and hail claims that don't involve suspected fraud.

**Standard authority (CHG §2.1)**
- Adjusters may set and change reserves only within their authority level, and for Level 1 (Associate Adjuster): up to $25,000 per claim.
- Reserves above your limit go up the chain: Level 2 (Senior Adjuster): up to $100,000 per claim, Level 3 (Claims Supervisor): up to $250,000 per claim, and above $250,000: Regional Claims Manager approval is required.

**Catastrophe exception (CHG §2.3)**
- During a declared catastrophe, Level 1 authority is temporarily raised to $50,000 for windstorm and hail claims, unless the claim involves suspected fraud. All three conditions must be met: a declared catastrophe, a windstorm or hail claim, and no suspected fraud. Otherwise your limit stays at $25,000.

**Related reserve requirements (CHG §2.2)**
- Reserves must be reviewed every 30 days and whenever material new information is received. A reserve change of more than 50% in a single adjustment requires a file note explaining the reason.

rows.question: What's my reserve authority as an associate adjuster on a hail claim during a catastrophe?
rows.answer:
**During a declared catastrophe, your Level 1 authority on a hail claim is $50,000, unless the claim involves suspected fraud.** If fraud is suspected, the temporary increase doesn't apply and your standard limit of $25,000 governs.

**Details:**

- **Standard authority (CHG §2.1):** Adjusters may set and change reserves only within their authority level, and Level 1 (Associate Adjuster): up to $25,000 per claim.
- **Catastrophe increase (CHG §2.3):** During a declared catastrophe, Level 1 authority is temporarily raised to $50,000 for windstorm and hail claims, unless the claim involves suspected fraud. The increase applies only when all of these are true:
  - The catastrophe has been declared.
  - The claim is a windstorm or hail claim.
  - No fraud is suspected.

  The increase is also temporary.
- **If the reserve exceeds your authority:** The next tier is Level 2 (Senior Adjuster): up to $100,000 per claim.

**Related reserve requirements (CHG §2.2):** Reserves must be reviewed every 30 days and whenever material new information is received. A reserve change of more than 50% in a single adjustment requires a file note explaining the reason.

rows.question: When do I need to refer a claim to SIU?
rows.answer:
**Refer a claim to SIU within 5 business days when two or more fraud indicators are present.** Per CHG §3.1, refer the claim to the Special Investigations Unit (SIU) within 5 business days if two or more of the following indicators are present:

- The policy was purchased or coverage increased within 60 days before the loss.
- The insured is unusually familiar with claims procedures or insurance terminology.
- The insured pressures for a quick settlement or offers to accept a lower amount in cash.
- Receipts or documents appear altered, or the insured cannot produce proof of ownership for high-value items.
- The loss occurs shortly after the insured disclosed financial difficulty.
- Multiple prior claims of a similar type within 36 months.

A single indicator alone doesn't trigger a mandatory referral under §3.1. You need at least two.

**After referral (CHG §3.2):** While a claim is under SIU review, continue to handle the claim in good faith and meet all regulatory deadlines. Do not disclose the SIU referral to the insured.

**Catastrophe authority (CHG §2.3):** Suspected fraud also affects your authority during catastrophes. During a declared catastrophe, Level 1 authority is temporarily raised to $50,000 for windstorm and hail claims, unless the claim involves suspected fraud. If a cat claim shows fraud indicators, the raised authority doesn't apply.

rows.question: How fast do I need to contact the insured on a bodily injury claim?
rows.answer:
On any claim involving bodily injury, you must make first contact with the insured **within 4 business hours** of first notice of loss (FNOL).

Per CHG §1.1, the assigned adjuster must make first contact with the insured within 24 hours of first notice of loss (FNOL) for property claims and within 4 business hours for any claim involving bodily injury. If a claim involves both property damage and bodily injury, the 4-business-hour standard applies because it covers "any claim involving bodily injury."

Also, document the contact attempt in the claim file even if unsuccessful.

rows.question: Is a 22-year-old roof eligible for replacement cost on new business?
rows.answer:
**No, not by default.** A 22-year-old roof exceeds the 20-year threshold for replacement cost on roof surfacing under UWG §1.1. It requires either an ACV roof endorsement or a favorable inspection.

**UWG §1.1 (Roof age), jurisdiction ALL:**
- New business is eligible for replacement cost on roof surfacing only if the roof is 20 years old or less.
- Roofs older than 20 years require an actual cash value roof endorsement or an inspection showing at least 5 years of remaining life.

For a 22-year-old roof, you have two options:
1. **Attach the ACV roof endorsement.** This places the roof surfacing on actual cash value.
2. **Order an inspection.** This option works only if the inspection shows at least 5 years of remaining life.

**Interpretation note:** §1.1 presents the inspection as an alternative to the ACV endorsement. However, the first sentence limits replacement cost eligibility to roofs "20 years old or less." The guideline doesn't say outright that a passing inspection restores full replacement cost on the roof surfacing. If you plan to write replacement cost on the roof based on an inspection alone, confirm that reading with underwriting management.

**Related new business requirement (UWG §2.1):** Apart from the roof, every new business and every third renewal requires a replacement cost estimate using the approved estimator. Coverage A must be at least 100% of the estimated replacement cost at new business.

rows.question: When do I refer a risk to a senior underwriter?
rows.answer:
Under UWG §3.1, refer a risk to a senior underwriter if it meets any one of three triggers: any risk with Coverage A above $1,500,000, any dwelling built before 1940, or any wildfire risk score of 8 or higher on the 10-point scale.

**Wildfire scores of 9 or 10:** These need more than a referral. Underwriters may not bind wildfire risk scores of 9 or 10 without Regional Underwriting Manager approval. A score of 8 needs a senior underwriter referral. A score of 9 or 10 also needs RUM approval before binding.

**Ineligible risks:** Referral is separate from eligibility. Some risks are ineligible outright under UWG §1.3 rather than referable. These include dwellings in foreclosure; dwellings vacant or unoccupied for more than 60 days; properties with an unfenced swimming pool; properties used for short-term rental more than 30 days per year without a home-sharing endorsement; and dwellings with knob-and-tube wiring.

rows.question: Can we write a house with a swimming pool?
rows.answer:
**It depends on whether the pool is fenced.** Under UWG §1.3, a property with an *unfenced* swimming pool is ineligible. A fenced pool is not listed as an ineligible risk in that section.

**Supporting detail (CHM-UWG 2026.1, §1.3, all jurisdictions):** The following are ineligible: dwellings in foreclosure; dwellings vacant or unoccupied for more than 60 days; properties with an unfenced swimming pool; properties used for short-term rental more than 30 days per year without a home-sharing endorsement; and dwellings with knob-and-tube wiring.

**Practical notes:**
- **Confirm the fencing.** The ineligibility applies only when the pool is unfenced. The provided guideline text doesn't define what counts as adequate fencing, such as height, gates, or self-latching requirements. If your process has a definition, check it against that.
- **Check the other §1.3 criteria.** A fenced pool doesn't make the risk eligible by itself. Make sure the dwelling also isn't:
  - in foreclosure
  - vacant or unoccupied for more than 60 days
  - used for short-term rental more than 30 days per year *without a home-sharing endorsement*
  - wired with knob-and-tube wiring
- **Other guidelines may apply.** Only §1.3 was provided. Other guideline sections may address pools, such as liability limits, diving boards, or slides. I can't confirm whether they exist from these sources.

This summarizes the guideline language and isn't a final eligibility decision on the risk.

rows.question: If my house burns down, do I have to list every item I lost to get paid for my belongings?
rows.answer:
**Generally yes, but California has an exception if the fire is tied to a declared state of emergency.** In that case, you can get an advance on your belongings without a full list. Otherwise, the standard policy requires an itemized inventory.

**The standard rule (base HO-3 policy)**
After a loss, one of your duties is to prepare an inventory of damaged personal property showing the quantity, description, actual cash value and amount of loss, with bills, receipts and related documents. Fire is covered for your belongings: the policy covers personal property for direct physical loss caused only by the following named perils: fire or lightning and others.

**The California exception (applies to you)**
In California, the state endorsement adds an advance payment, but only if the fire is a covered total loss tied to a declared state of emergency, such as a wildfire disaster declaration. In that situation, we will offer a payment under Coverage C of no less than 30% of the Coverage C limit, up to $250,000, without requiring an itemized inventory.

For example, if your belongings (Coverage C) limit were $200,000, the advance would be at least $60,000 with no itemized list. Your actual limit is shown on your Declarations page.

Some things to keep in mind:
- **It depends on the cause.** If your house burns down in a fire that isn't linked to a declared state of emergency, this exception doesn't apply, and the standard inventory requirement does.
- **It's an advance, not necessarily your full payment.** The endorsement waives the list for this advance payment. It doesn't say the list is waived for amounts beyond it. If your losses exceed the advance, expect that you may still need to document them.
- **Related California benefit.** For a total loss tied to a declared state of emergency, you also get more time to claim full replacement cost. The 180-day period in HO-3 Section 6.3 to make a claim for additional replacement cost is replaced with a period of no less than 36 months from the date of the first actual cash value payment.

Whatever the cause, you should still give prompt notice to us or our agent. This explains what the policy language says. It isn't a coverage decision; your claim will be evaluated on its facts.

rows.question: After a total loss, how long do I have to collect the rest of the replacement cost?
rows.answer:
**It depends on whether your total loss relates to a declared state of emergency.** If it does, California gives you at least 36 months from your first actual cash value payment. If it doesn't, the standard policy deadline is 180 days after the loss.

**How it works**

Your policy first pays the actual cash value (the depreciated value) of your home, then the rest of the replacement cost once you rebuild. The base policy says we will pay no more than actual cash value until actual repair or replacement is complete. You may make a claim on an actual cash value basis and then make a claim for any additional replacement cost within 180 days after the loss.

**California's longer deadline for declared emergencies**

Because your home is in California, the California endorsement changes this deadline, but only for emergency-related total losses. For a total loss relating to a declared state of emergency, the 180-day period in HO-3 Section 6.3 to make a claim for additional replacement cost is replaced with a period of no less than 36 months from the date of the first actual cash value payment.

- **Total loss related to a declared state of emergency** (for example, a wildfire with an official emergency declaration): you have at least 36 months from your first actual cash value payment.
- **Total loss not related to a declared state of emergency:** the endorsement doesn't apply, so the 180-day deadline from the date of loss still applies.

**Other California benefits that may matter to you**

- **Rebuilding somewhere else:** If you choose to rebuild or replace the dwelling at a location other than the residence premises, we will pay the replacement cost of the dwelling, up to the Coverage A limit, measured as the cost to rebuild at the original residence premises. The value of the land at the new location is not included.
- **Advance payment for your belongings, only for emergency-related total losses:** In the event of a covered total loss of the dwelling relating to a declared state of emergency, we will offer a payment under Coverage C of no less than 30% of the Coverage C limit, up to $250,000, without requiring an itemized inventory.

The amount you can collect also depends on how much insurance you carry compared with your home's full replacement cost. Your Declarations page and your claim details will settle which deadline applies, so confirm it with your adjuster. This explains your policy language. It isn't a coverage decision or a promise of payment.

rows.question: Is mold from a slow leak covered?
rows.answer:
**It depends on how long the leak lasted and whether it counts as a covered peril.** Your policy pays for mold only when the mold results from a covered peril, and a slow leak lasting 14 or more days is generally not one.

**Mold coverage and its limit**
Your policy says it will pay up to $10,000 in total for direct physical loss caused by fungi, mold, wet or dry rot, or bacteria, including the cost to remove it and to tear out and replace covered property to gain access, but only when the fungi or rot results from a covered peril, such as a sudden pipe burst. This is the most we will pay regardless of the number of locations or claims during the policy period.

**Why a slow leak is different**
The policy lists certain causes of loss it does not insure against, including continuous or repeated seepage or leakage of water or steam over a period of 14 or more days from within a plumbing, heating or air conditioning system or household appliance. If your leak went on for 14 days or more, it likely isn't a covered peril. In that case, the $10,000 mold coverage would not apply, because that coverage applies only when the mold results from a covered peril.

**Water damage from the leak**
Even when the leak itself falls into that list, the policy says: If any of these cause water damage not otherwise excluded, we cover the resulting water damage, including the cost of tearing out and replacing part of the building to access the system, but not the system or appliance itself. This sentence is about water damage. These excerpts don't say whether it also extends to mold, so I can't confirm that.

**What determines the outcome**
- **How long the leak continued:** 14 or more days falls under the listed non-covered seepage.
- **What caused it:** for example, whether it came from wear and tear or deterioration, wear and tear, marring, deterioration, mechanical breakdown, latent defect, or inherent vice is also on that list.

This explains what the policy language says. It isn't a coverage decision. If you have mold damage, report the claim so an adjuster can review the facts, including how long the leak lasted and what caused it.

rows.question: My pipes froze while I was away for the winter. Is that covered?
rows.answer:
**It depends on whether you took reasonable steps to protect the pipes before you left.** Your homeowners policy doesn't cover frozen pipes while the home is vacant or unoccupied, unless you kept the heat on or shut off the water and drained the system. I can't make a final coverage decision, but here's what the policy language says.

**The frozen pipes themselves (your house and other structures)**
Your policy covers your dwelling against direct physical loss, except for certain listed causes. One of those is freezing of a plumbing system while the dwelling is vacant or unoccupied, unless you used reasonable care to maintain heat or shut off the water supply and drain the system. So the key questions are:
- Did you keep the heat on while you were away?
- Or did you shut off the water and drain the pipes?

If you did either, this exclusion shouldn't apply. If you didn't, damage from the freezing likely wouldn't be covered.

**Water damage caused by the frozen pipes**
If any of these cause water damage not otherwise excluded, we cover the resulting water damage, including the cost of tearing out and replacing part of the building to access the system, but not the system or appliance itself. So resulting water damage may be covered as long as it isn't excluded elsewhere in the policy. Repairing the burst pipe itself isn't covered under this provision.

One more thing to know if a leak continued while you were gone: the policy also excludes continuous or repeated seepage or leakage of water or steam over a period of 14 or more days from within a plumbing, heating or air conditioning system or household appliance. How long the water was leaking could matter.

**Your belongings (furniture, clothing, etc.)**
Personal property is covered only for specific listed causes, and the list includes accidental discharge or overflow of water or steam and freezing.

**Mold, if it develops**
The policy will pay up to $10,000 in total for direct physical loss caused by fungi, mold, wet or dry rot, or bacteria, including the cost to remove it and to tear out and replace covered property to gain access, but only when the fungi or rot results from a covered peril, such as a sudden pipe burst.

**Next steps:** When you report the claim, be ready to explain what you did to protect the home before leaving, such as the thermostat setting or whether the water was shut off and the pipes drained. Also be ready to say roughly when the damage likely happened. Those facts will drive the coverage decision.

rows.question: Will hail damage to my roof be paid at replacement cost?
rows.answer:
**It depends mainly on how old your roof is, and whether the damage is only cosmetic.** In Texas, the Windstorm and Hail Deductible Endorsement changes how hail damage to roofs is handled compared with the standard HO-3 policy.

**Roof age**
- **Roofs older than 15 years:** Loss to roof surfacing caused by windstorm or hail is settled at actual cash value, not replacement cost, if the roof surfacing is more than 15 years old at the time of loss. Actual cash value takes depreciation (wear and age) into account, so the payment would typically be less than the cost of a new roof.
- **Roofs 15 years old or less:** Roof surfacing 15 years old or less is settled under HO-3 Section 6.3. That section provides replacement cost, which means the cost to repair or replace damaged property with material of like kind and quality, for the same use, without deduction for depreciation.

**Conditions on replacement cost (for roofs 15 years old or less)**
- **Your coverage amount:** Full replacement cost applies only if, at the time of loss, the amount of insurance on the damaged building is 80% or more of its full replacement cost. If it is less than 80%, we will pay the greater of the actual cash value of the damaged part or that proportion of the cost to repair or replace that the limit of insurance bears to 80% of the replacement cost. Your Declarations page shows your coverage amount.
- **Completing the repair:** We will pay no more than actual cash value until actual repair or replacement is complete. You may make a claim on an actual cash value basis and then make a claim for any additional replacement cost within 180 days after the loss.

**Cosmetic hail damage is not covered at all**
Regardless of roof age, the Texas endorsement says we do not cover cosmetic damage to roof surfacing caused by hail. Cosmetic damage means marring, pitting or denting that changes the appearance of the roof surface but does not prevent the roof from continuing to function as a barrier to water entering the dwelling, and does not shorten the expected life of the roof.

**Related help after a hail loss**
- **Temporary repairs:** When your property is damaged by a covered peril, the policy pays the reasonable cost incurred by you for necessary measures taken solely to protect covered property that is damaged by a covered peril from further damage, such as tarping a damaged roof or boarding broken windows. Keep receipts for these expenses.
- **Debris removal:** We will pay your reasonable expense for the removal of debris of covered property if a covered peril causes the loss.

This explains what the policy language says. The actual outcome of your claim will depend on your roof's age at the time of loss, your coverage amount compared with your home's replacement cost, and the adjuster's assessment of whether the damage is functional or cosmetic.

rows.answer:

**What the policy says about transportation expenses**

The temporary transportation benefit is tied to theft. The policy will pay without application of a deductible, up to $20 per day, to a maximum of $600, for temporary transportation expenses incurred by you because of the total theft of your covered auto. Even then, it pays only expenses incurred during the period beginning 48 hours after the theft and ending when your covered auto is returned or we pay for its loss.

Nothing in the sections I have extends this benefit to a car in the shop after an accident.

**Possible Rental Reimbursement endorsement**

The policy refers to a Rental Reimbursement endorsement: If a Rental Reimbursement endorsement is shown in the Declarations, its daily and maximum limits apply instead. That sentence only says the endorsement's limits replace the theft benefit's limits. I don't have the endorsement's own wording, so I can't tell you whether it covers rentals during crash repairs.

rows.question: Will you pay for building code upgrades when I rebuild?
rows.answer:
**Generally no. The standard homeowners policy does not pay the extra cost of meeting building codes when you rebuild, unless your policy includes an Ordinance or Law endorsement listed on your Declarations page.**

The policy says: "We do not cover the increased cost of construction required by any ordinance or law regulating the construction, repair or demolition of a building, except as provided by an Ordinance or Law endorsement if shown in the Declarations."

**What this means for you:**
- **If your Declarations page shows an Ordinance or Law endorsement:** That endorsement may cover some or all of the extra cost of code upgrades. How much depends on its terms and limits, which aren't in the material I have.
- **If it doesn't:** The extra cost of bringing the home up to current code isn't covered under the base policy.

**How the rebuild itself is paid (separate from code upgrades):**
- Damaged buildings are settled at replacement cost without deduction for depreciation. You get full repair or replacement cost, up to your limit, only if your coverage amount is high enough: if, at the time of loss, the amount of insurance on the damaged building is 80% or more of its full replacement cost, we will pay the cost to repair or replace, up to the limit of liability. If your coverage is below that 80% level, the payment may be reduced.
- We will pay no more than actual cash value until actual repair or replacement is complete. You can make a claim on an actual cash value basis and then make a claim for any additional replacement cost within 180 days after the loss.

**Next step:** Check your Declarations page for an Ordinance or Law endorsement, or ask your agent whether you have it. This explains the policy language only. Whether a particular claim is paid depends on the facts of your loss and your actual policy.

rows.question: Can an associate adjuster set a $40,000 reserve on a hail claim?
rows.answer:
**It depends on whether a catastrophe has been declared.** Ordinarily, an associate adjuster cannot set a $40,000 reserve. The exception is a declared catastrophe where the claim involves no suspected fraud.

**Standard authority (CHG §2.1):** Adjusters may set and change reserves only within their authority level, and Level 1 (Associate Adjuster): up to $25,000 per claim. A $40,000 reserve exceeds that. It falls within Level 2 (Senior Adjuster): up to $100,000 per claim.

**Catastrophe exception (CHG §2.3):** During a declared catastrophe, Level 1 authority is temporarily raised to $50,000 for windstorm and hail claims, unless the claim involves suspected fraud. A hail claim qualifies by peril type. So an associate adjuster may set the $40,000 reserve only if:
- the claim arises during a declared catastrophe, **and**
- the claim does not involve suspected fraud.

If either condition isn't met, the reserve needs Senior Adjuster (Level 2) authority or higher.

**Related reminder (CHG §2.2):** If the $40,000 figure is an adjustment to an existing reserve, note that a reserve change of more than 50% in a single adjustment requires a file note explaining the reason.

rows.question: My detached garage burned down. Is it covered and up to what amount?
rows.answer:
**Your detached garage is the type of structure your policy covers under Coverage B, and the limit is generally 10% of your dwelling (Coverage A) limit, unless your Declarations page shows a different amount.** The exact dollar figure depends on the limits on your Declarations page, which I don't have. This explains what the policy language says. It isn't a final coverage decision.

**What's covered**
- The policy covers other structures on the residence premises set apart from the dwelling by clear space, such as a detached garage, fence or shed.
- One exception applies: We do not cover other structures rented to any person who is not a tenant of the dwelling, unless used solely as a private garage. If you rent the garage to someone who doesn't live in your home, it's covered only if it's used solely as a private garage.
- The excerpts I have don't list which causes of loss are covered for other structures. Whether this fire is covered will depend on that policy language and the facts of the loss.

**How much**
- The limit for Coverage B is 10% of the Coverage A limit unless a different limit is shown in the Declarations. For example, if your dwelling limit is $300,000, the garage limit would be $30,000, unless your Declarations page shows something different.
- **Deductible:** we will pay only that part of the total of all loss payable that exceeds the deductible amount shown in the Declarations.

**Cleanup costs (debris removal)**
- The policy will pay your reasonable expense for the removal of debris of covered property if a covered peril causes the loss.
- This expense is included in the limit of liability that applies to the damaged property. If the amount to be paid for the actual damage plus debris removal exceeds the limit, an additional 5% of that limit is available for debris removal. This extra 5% applies only if the loss was caused by a covered peril.

**Belongings stored in the garage**
- Personal property, such as tools or stored items, falls under a separate coverage (Coverage C). That coverage applies for direct physical loss caused only by the following named perils: fire or lightning and other listed perils. Fire is one of the named perils for your belongings.

To find your exact limits and deductible, check your Declarations page for your Coverage A and Coverage B amounts.

rows.question: Will you pay for the tarp I put on my roof after the storm?
rows.answer:
**Generally yes, as long as the storm damage to your roof is from a covered peril.** Your homeowners policy says we will pay the reasonable cost incurred by you for necessary measures taken solely to protect covered property that is damaged by a covered peril from further damage, such as tarping a damaged roof or boarding broken windows.

- **The cost being reasonable and necessary.** The policy pays the reasonable cost of measures needed solely to protect the property from further damage.

- **Keep your receipts.** The policy says to keep receipts for these expenses.
- **Report the loss promptly.** After a loss you must give prompt notice to us or our agent.

rows.question: Sewage came up through my basement drain. Covered?
rows.answer:
**Under the standard HO-3 form, sewage backing up through a drain is generally not covered, unless your policy includes a water backup endorsement.**

**What the base policy says:** Among its water exclusions, the HO-3 states that we do not cover loss caused by: ... water or water-borne material that backs up through sewers or drains or overflows from a sump pump. Sewage coming up through a basement drain falls within that language.

**The possible exception:** The same section notes that water backup coverage is available by endorsement with a sublimit. So whether you have any coverage depends on:
- **Whether you bought the water backup endorsement.** Check your Declarations page for it.
- **The sublimit.** If you have the endorsement, coverage would be capped at a lower dollar amount specific to that endorsement. The documents I have don't show the amount, so check your Declarations or the endorsement itself.

**A related point:** If the water came from flooding outside rather than a sewer or drain backup, that is a separate exclusion. Flood coverage is available only through a separate flood policy.

rows.question: Can you cancel my car insurance after I've had it for six months?
rows.answer:
**Yes, but only for specific reasons.** Since your policy has been in effect for more than 60 days, we will cancel only for nonpayment of premium, or if your driver's license or that of any driver who lives with you or customarily uses your covered auto has been suspended or revoked, or if the policy was obtained through material misrepresentation.

**How you'd be notified:**
- We may cancel this policy by mailing notice to the named insured.
- If the reason is nonpayment of premium, you'd get at least 10 days' notice. For any other allowed reason, such as a suspended or revoked license or material misrepresentation, you'd get at least 20 days' notice. The policy says: Notice for nonpayment is at least 10 days; for any other reason, at least 20 days.

**For comparison:** the rules are looser in a policy's early days. If the policy has been in effect less than 60 days, we will give at least 10 days notice. At that stage, the reasons are not limited to the ones listed above.

This explains what the policy language says. It is not a decision about any particular situation. If you've received a cancellation notice or are worried about one, contact your agent to talk through the details.

rows.question: My tires got damaged by a pothole. Will collision pay?
rows.answer:
**Probably not, if only the tires were damaged.** The policy excludes road damage to tires when the damage is limited to the tires. The policy lists among its physical damage exclusions: We will not pay for: Damage due and confined to wear and tear, freezing, mechanical or electrical breakdown or failure, or road damage to tires.

**What it depends on:**

- **Whether the damage went beyond the tires.** The exclusion covers damage that is "due and confined to" road damage to tires. If the pothole also damaged other parts, such as a wheel, rim, or suspension, those other parts aren't covered by the wording of this exclusion. The policy defines "Collision" means the upset of your covered auto or a non-owned auto or their impact with another vehicle or object. These sections don't say whether hitting a pothole counts as impact with an "object." Your claims adjuster would decide how that damage is treated.
- **Whether you have Collision Coverage.** The policy pays for collision losses only if the Declarations indicate that Collision Coverage is provided. Check your Declarations page.
- **Your deductible.** Any covered payment is minus any applicable deductible shown in the Declarations.

**How a covered loss would be paid:** Payment is limited to the lesser of the actual cash value of the stolen or damaged property, or the amount necessary to repair or replace the property with other property of like kind and quality.

This is what the policy language says, not a final coverage decision. If other parts of your car were damaged, report the claim so an adjuster can review it.

rows.question: How long after a hailstorm can I still file a claim?
rows.answer:
**In Texas, you have one year from the date of the hailstorm to report your claim, unless there's good cause for reporting later.** Under the Texas Windstorm and Hail Deductible Endorsement, a claim for windstorm or hail damage must be reported to us within one year after the date of the windstorm or hail event, unless good cause exists for later reporting. This applies if that endorsement is part of your policy, and your policy documents will show that.

**Report as soon as you can.** The standard homeowners policy also requires you to give prompt notice to us or our agent. Early reporting is safer than waiting until the deadline.

**Other deadlines to know about:**
- **Inspection:** We will inspect the damage within 15 days after receiving notice of the claim, unless a catastrophe has been declared, in which case the inspection period may be extended by 15 days.
- **Proof of loss:** You must send to us, within 60 days after our request, your signed, sworn proof of loss.
- **Replacement cost:** You may make a claim on an actual cash value basis and then make a claim for any additional replacement cost within 180 days after the loss.

**After the storm, you should also:** protect the property from further damage and make reasonable and necessary repairs to protect it.

This explains what the policy language says. Whether a particular claim is covered depends on the details of the loss and your policy.

rows.question: The insured wants to invoke appraisal. What's my deadline to respond?
rows.answer:
You have **two deadlines**: acknowledge the appraisal request in writing within 5 business days, and name the company appraiser within 20 days of receiving the insured's written request.

**Internal guideline (CHG §4.3):** If the insured invokes appraisal, acknowledge the request in writing within 5 business days and name the company appraiser within the 20-day window in HO-3 Section 6.5.

**Policy language (HO-3 §6.5):**
- **When appraisal applies:** If you and we fail to agree on the amount of loss, either may demand an appraisal of the loss. Appraisal is limited to disputes over the amount of loss.
- **When the 20 days start:** Each party will choose a competent and impartial appraiser within 20 days after receiving a written request from the other. The clock starts when the company receives the insured's *written* request. If the insured has only asked verbally, you may want to confirm whether a written demand has been received.
- **What happens next:** The two appraisers will choose an umpire. A decision agreed to by any two will set the amount of loss. Each party pays its own appraiser and shares equally the expense of the umpire.

No state endorsement applies here, so the base HO-3 20-day window governs.
